scripts.summary: Reps run the discovery half well (why now on 90% of calls, doubt question 81%, pillars 64 to 81%) but the back half is improvised: money is never qualified before the pitch (0 of 55 calls), 26 of 47 pitched calls quoted an off-sheet price (the $1,000 first session on 15, the $2,400 starter on 9), 37 of 55 carried an outcome promise such as '80% find a partner', and next steps before price were run in full on 6 of 47. The three changes that matter most: lock prices to $3,600 / $7,200 / $14,000 with Tier 1.5 as the planned lower option, add a budget check before the pitch, and add the missing safety sections (recording disclosure, crisis pause, prospect-only financing applications). Nov 17 edit: no change is detectable. playbook_closer.json already cites the 2026-11-17 edit and was written at 01:25 UTC on 18 Nov, after the 19:19 UTC edit; every one of its 51 checks and 3 prices matches the current text, and Drive returned no revision history. Text in the current doc that the playbook does not score: the 'when did you realize / specific event' probes, 'How long has it been like this for you?' in Current Situation, the optional proof point in Transition, the pillar working-names note, and the 'Tier 2/3' delivery line. All 55 analysed calls (5 Jun to 11 Nov) predate the edit, so the patches target the current text.

patches.script_says: Recommend the fit based on discovery, anchor it, then SHUT UP.
patches.reality: 26 of 47 pitched calls (55%) quoted at least one price that is not on the sheet, 15 distinct prices in all. The two that recur: a $1,000 'first call / first session with Kim' on 15 calls and a $2,400 '6 weeks, 4 sessions' or 'first month' starter on 9 calls. Also $13,900 and $13,997 for the $14,000 tier, $3,400, $3,500, $3,800 and $4,000 for the $3,600 tier, and $500 or $337 entries. Calls with an off-sheet price closed 2 of 26 (8%); pitched calls that stayed on the sheet closed 5 of 21 (24%). The $1,000 offer turned into a $100 deposit on one call and a 'Foundation Program' at $2,400 in the CRM on another.
patches.what_works: The won calls mostly stayed on one sheet price and stopped talking: recuYUaiJrHqjgDoh, recDSlt2076AjpWME and recHhuHL21q8NAwRy closed on sanctioned tiers. Where the prospect asked to pay for one session first (recQgbOLAOMtxKfce), the close came from a 1 to 10 check and a payment split, not a new product.
patches.change: Add a hard rule under TIER MAPPING: the only prices a closer says are $3,600, $7,200 and $14,000. No trial calls, deposits for a single session, 6-week starters, first-month options or rounded numbers. If a prospect asks to try one session first, use the trial-request lines below. Anything else goes to Mitch before it is said on a call.
new_lines: [Rule] The only three prices you say on a call are $3,600, $7,200 and $14,000. Never quote a single session, a deposit for one call, a 6-week or first-month option, or a number you round.

If they ask to pay for one session first: "I get why you'd want to feel it out first. Kim doesn't sell single sessions, because one hour can't change how you show up. What the three months does is give you the first few weeks to feel the difference. What would you need to see in those first weeks to know it's working?"
If they ask for something cheaper: "The option that keeps Kim one on one with you at a lower investment is the bi-weekly three months at $3,600. Would that fit better?"

patches.reality: Money was qualified before the pitch on 0 of 55 calls, won or lost. The script has no step for it: the first time money comes up is the price. Price/budget objections came up 57 times on 37 of 55 calls, 49 of them after the price, and were resolved 16% of the time. The setters do not fill the gap: the means gate was weak or missed on 22 of 28 setter calls, and setters did not give the sanctioned anchor on 16 of the 18 calls where they named a price.
patches.what_works: Nothing to copy before the pitch: no call did it. After the price, the won calls used 'money aside, does the process feel right' (C13a hit on 5 of 7 won calls).
patches.change: Add a short budget check at the end of TIE DOWN DISCOVERY, before TRANSITION. It asks how they would fund it, not whether they like the price, and it does not reveal a number. If they say they have no way to invest anything, stop and do not pitch.
new_lines: Before I walk you through how Kim would work with you, one practical question so I point you at the right option. (Setter) mentioned working with Kim is an investment in the four figures. If this turns out to be exactly what you need, how would you normally handle something like that: pay upfront, spread it over a few months, or would you need to look at financing?

[If they say they have no income or no way to invest anything] I really appreciate you being honest. I don't want to walk you through something that only adds pressure right now. Let's get you the free resources and reconnect when the timing is better. Fair?

patches.script_says: [Note: dating outcomes can't be guaranteed. Promise the process and the visible near-term change, the relationship is the destination, not a guarantee.]
patches.reality: 37 of 55 calls (67%) carried an outcome promise, with 40 outcome-promise flags. 28 calls cite a success rate: '80% find a partner in the first year' or '50% within six months and 78% within 12 months', said in near-identical words by different reps. 13 calls promise 'at least two dates a week'. Others say '100%' or 'she's going to help you find your person'. The note in the script has no approved line to replace these, so reps use the stats. Promises did not lift the close rate: 5 of 37 calls with a promise closed (14%) against 2 of 18 without.
patches.what_works: The script's own line works when used: 'visible near-term change' (new matches, conversations that go somewhere, real dates). C9a, the no-guarantee promise, was fully hit on only 3 calls.
patches.change: Turn the note into a rule with banned phrases and one approved proof line. Ban any percentage of clients finding a partner, any dates-per-week number, '100%', 'she will get you there'. Mitch decides whether the 50%/78% figure is real and documented; until then it is not said.
new_lines: [Never say] any percentage of clients who find a partner, any number of dates per week, '100%', 'guaranteed', or 'she'll get you your person'.

I can't promise you a relationship, and nobody honest can. What I can tell you is what changes: within the first few weeks most people see different responses, because the profile, the messaging and how you show up all get fixed. The relationship is where this leads, and Kim's job is to get you showing up as the person who gets there.

On 4 calls the prospect raised the recording first, and on 3 calls reps promised it would be discarded or deleted, which did not happen (the recordings are in this audit). [If they say no] No problem, I'll stop the recording now. [Stop it, then carry on.]

patches.reality: The script has no financing section, and 23 of 55 calls offered a third-party financing partner (ClarityPay on 17). Reps run the application live: on recGKZs9W2uilOrBj the rep had the prospect read his Social Security number and income aloud on a recorded call and typed them in on her own shared screen; on recs3px0F2ml4Yv7v the rep told a prospect who earns $18,000 to put at least $30,000. Reps also told prospects financing had 'no extra cost' while the offer carried 17% APR and a 5% fee, and ran screen-shared credit checks after 'I can't afford it' (reck9JVOjrzpNKQQY, recC4gM25DJe88Ryw).

The rep never hears or types an SSN, date of birth or income, never suggests a number, and reads the APR and total cost back before they sign. [Never] ask for a Social Security number, date of birth or income out loud, type a prospect's details yourself, suggest what income to enter, or run a credit check after they have said they can't afford it.

patches.section: WHY NOW & COST: THE MOST IMPORTANT PART OF THE CALL
patches.script_says: Can I ask you something real? … What's this actually been costing you? Not just in dating … like how does it spill into the rest of your life?
patches.reality: The cost questions open up heavy disclosures and the script has nothing for them. 14 of 55 calls (25%) carry a wellbeing-risk flag: suicidal history ('I haven't killed myself yet'), rape and assault, PTSD, depression with medication changes. On none of them did the rep pause or check in, and on several the disclosure was used as cost-of-inaction leverage. 1 of the 14 closed. 4 calls also blurred coaching with therapy (one prospect left thinking Kim is a licensed therapist who takes insurance).
patches.what_works: Nothing to copy from the calls.
patches.change: Add a pause branch right after the cost questions: if they mention self-harm, suicide, abuse, assault or a mental-health crisis, stop selling, check in, and point them to support. If there is any current risk, end the sales part of the call. Never use the disclosure as a reason to buy. Add one line saying Kim is a dating coach, not a therapist.
new_lines: [If they mention self-harm, suicide, abuse, assault or a current crisis] Thank you for trusting me with that. I want to pause the dating stuff for a second. How are you doing right now, today?

[If there is any current risk] I'm really glad you told me. This matters more than anything we were going to talk about. If you're in the US you can call or text 988 any time, and if you're working with a therapist, please let them know too. Let's pick this conversation up another time.
[Always] Kim is a dating and relationship coach, not a therapist, and this isn't a replacement for therapy. Lots of her clients do both.
[Never] use something painful they shared as a reason to decide today.

evidence.quote: I think I've broken it, I think. I think I'm okay. I haven't killed myself yet, so…
I would have to increase my medication dosage
It's, you know, life and death-ish, kind of in the balance type of thing.
she's a licensed therapist. So I don't know. Would she take insurance?

patches.reality: The note sends closers to $7,200 for prospects the setter anchored at 'low to mid four figures', which $7,200 is not. The $3,600 bi-weekly tier, the one that matches that anchor, was quoted on only 4 calls; reps instead invented $3,400 to $4,000 versions or the $1,000 and $2,400 starters (MC-01). On recd2WbFpUUNdfhxj the prospect asked if $7,200 was the only option, was told yes, and was then offered ad-hoc discounts. On recuYUaiJrHqjgDoh the prospect said the setter had set a $3,000 to $4,000 expectation, and the closer quoted $14,000.
patches.what_works: recuYUaiJrHqjgDoh closed once the rep moved to the three-month bi-weekly option after financing was declined.
patches.change: Rewrite the note: Tier 1 ($7,200) is the default when they can fund it; when the budget check (MC-02) or the price reaction says the budget is lower, go straight to Tier 1.5 at $3,600 as the planned second option, not a discount.
new_lines: [Note] Recommend Tier 1 ($7,200) when their answer to the budget question says they can fund it. If their budget is clearly lower, recommend Tier 1.5 ($3,600) from the start. Tier 1.5 is the planned lower option, so never invent a price between them.

patches.reality: The tier map lists Tier 1.5, Tier 1 and Tier 2, all with 1:1 calls, but DELIVERY says 1:1 is only for 'Tier 2/3'. Reps are confused by the labels: on 6 calls the rep called the $14,000 six-month program 'tier one' or 'the first tier', so prospects left thinking the entry price is $14,000 (1 of the 6 closed). On recC5UEp94Pe8qvhW and recrae8WpaHedIgrN, $7,200 was described as 'weekly or bi-weekly', which is the $3,600 tier. One rep told a prospect there is no group component.
patches.what_works: Calls where the rep named the option by what it is (three months weekly, three months every other week, six months weekly) had no label confusion.
patches.change: Drop tier numbers from anything said to a prospect. Name each option by length and cadence. Fix DELIVERY so 1:1 with Kim is in every option and the group calls, library and community are in every option.
new_lines: Every option includes the twice-weekly group calls, the full library, the community, and private one-on-one calls with Kim. The only difference is how often you're with Kim and for how long: three months every other week, three months every week, or six months every week.

patches.script_says: [Paint the picture of getting started before they hear the number. This raises certainty.]
patches.reality: Run fully on 6 of 47 pitched calls (13%) and partly on 7; most reps go from the pillars or the temperature check straight to the number. Where it was run in full, 2 of 6 closed (33%); everywhere else 5 of 41 (12%). Small sample, but it points the same way as the script.
patches.what_works: recuYUaiJrHqjgDoh and recDSlt2076AjpWME (both won) said it almost word for word: immediate access to the library, then the first session with Kim booked.
patches.change: Keep the step and make it a short script with a check question so it is not skipped. Say it right after the temperature check, every time.
new_lines: Cool. So here's what happens once you're in. Today you get access to the full library and the community, and you're on the next group call this week.

Then we get your first one-on-one with Kim booked in the next few days, so she can look at your (profile / situationship / what you told me) straight away. You'd basically start showing up differently this week. How does that sound?

patches.script_says: So on a scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is "this isn't for me" and 10 is "this is exactly what I've been looking for" … where are you, honestly?
patches.reality: Reps ask how they feel about the process (hit on 32 of 47), but on 24 of 47 pitched calls the price came before the temperature check was finished. The 1 to 10 scale was used on 8 of 37 calls where the answer was uncertain; 'I think so' is usually taken as a yes. Order alone did not decide outcomes (5 of 24 priced-first calls closed, 2 of 23 others), but handling what kept them from a 9 or 10 (C10c) was done on every won call where it applied and on 32% of the rest.
patches.what_works: Won calls named the hesitation: recHhuHL21q8NAwRy ('You said I think so, which sounds, like, not 100% certain') and recuYUaiJrHqjgDoh ('You said the library is kind of keeping you from being a 10?').
patches.change: Make 'I think so', 'probably' or 'yeah' a trigger for the 1 to 10 question, and do not move to NEXT STEPS or price until whatever is below a 9 has been answered.
new_lines: You said 'I think so'. That's totally fine, and I'd rather know now. On a scale of 1 to 10, where are you, honestly?
What would need to be true for that to be a 9 or 10?
[Do not go to Next Steps or price until that is answered.]

evidence.quote: You said I think so, which sounds, like, not 100% certain, which is fine. Is there anything that you don't think or you're unsure of that, like, won't be helpful for you?
You said the library is kind of keeping you from being a 10?

patches.script_says: So in other words, this isn't a 'should I do this' thing, it's more of a 'how do I make this work' thing?
patches.reality: Reps take money off the table (C13a hit on 24 of 50) but rarely land the tie-down: hit on 2 of 51, partly on 17. Payment plans or financing were offered on 38 of 47 pitched calls, often to prospects who were unsure about the process, which the script forbids (C13c missed on 20 of 50). Price objections were resolved 16% of the time. C13b was run on 50% of won calls and 16% of the rest.
patches.what_works: recuYUaiJrHqjgDoh (won) said the tie-down nearly word for word before talking payments. recfCGXhoVRpBHdtY (won) set the cost against the outcome.
patches.change: Add the next line after the tie-down: only when they agree it is a 'how' question do you offer the sanctioned split or financing. If they hesitate, go back to the 1 to 10, not to a plan.
new_lines: So in other words, this isn't a 'should I do this' thing, it's more of a 'how do I make this work' thing?
[If yes] Okay. Then let's look at how. Would it be easier to do it in one payment, or split across the three months?
[If they hesitate] That's fine. Then it's not really about the money yet. On a scale of 1 to 10, where are you on the process itself?

patches.reality: The script has no branch for a prospect who asks for time or says no. 27 conduct flags on 25 calls, 5 of them high or critical: reps kept pressing after repeated requests for 24 hours, told prospects they could not sleep on it, used 'limited spots' to ask for deposits, asked prospects to check bank accounts or share finances live, and on one call kept a prospect on after he said three times it would not work. 'Think about it' was raised 32 times on 29 calls and resolved 6% of the time, so the pressure did not convert.
patches.what_works: recfCGXhoVRpBHdtY (won) asked one clear question before letting them go: 'before you kind of go and think about it, do you feel like this process would actually help you'.
patches.change: Add a respect-the-no branch: ask once what is behind the request for time, answer it, then book a short follow-up. Ban fake scarcity, live bank or finance checks, and a second push after a clear no.
new_lines: Of course. Before you go and think, can I ask what specifically you want to think through: the process, the money, or talking it over with someone?
[Answer that one thing, then] That makes sense. Let's put 15 minutes in for (day) at (time), so you can come back with a yes or a no and it doesn't drift. Does that work?
[Never] say spots are limited unless Mitch has confirmed it, ask them to check a bank account or share their finances on screen, or ask again after a clear no.

scripts.summary: Setters follow the opening and core discovery (intro, anchor to the opt-in, biggest problem and dig-in run on 78 to 92% of calls) but the back half breaks: 16 of 18 price mentions were off the 'low to mid four figures' anchor, the money answer is weak or missing on 22 of 28 calls, and no booking had the invite accepted live. The three changes: one true price anchor said word for word, drop the credit-score DQ for a yes/no financing question, and add invite-accepted-live plus a Zoom check and a word to reschedule. All 28 recorded setter calls (9 Sep to 16 Nov) predate the 17 Nov edit. No change is detectable against playbook_setter.json, which was built after the edit and already encodes the 650 credit rule and the low-to-mid anchor.

patches.script_says: It depends entirely on the plan you come up with with our advisor, how many sessions you end up having with Kim, the timeline, etc … but for most people it ends up being in the low to mid four figure range
patches.reality: Of 28 recorded setter calls (27 by Emily), a price was said on 18 and 16 of those were outside the anchor: 'mid to high four figures' on 11 calls, a specific '5,000 to 9,000' on 6 (said or confirmed), and '500 to 700' for a single conversation with Kim on 1. Only 2 used 'low to mid' or 'mid four figures'. The drift has a cause: the anchor does not match the offer ($3,600, $7,200, $14,000), and a texted lead who heard 'low to mid four figures' said he would not have taken the call had he known it was $7,200. Of 10 CRM bookings from these calls, 4 showed and 0 closed.
patches.what_works: Texts sent from the scripts used the anchor word for word (12 threads), so the wording is not the problem; the mismatch with the real prices is.
patches.change: Mitch picks one anchor that is true for the offer and every setter script uses it word for word. Until then, setters use the current line exactly and never give a dollar figure, a 'five to nine' range or a per-session price. Suggested anchor if Mitch approves: 'starts in the mid four figures'.
new_lines: It depends on how much one-on-one time with Kim makes sense for you, but most people invest somewhere in the low to mid four figures. I'm not asking you to commit to anything today. If it's the right fit, is that something that would be feasible for you?

[If they ask for an exact number] The advisor will map that out with you, because it depends on how often you'd be working with Kim. What I can tell you is it's a four-figure investment, so I just want to make sure that's realistic before we book.
[Never say] 'mid to high four figures', a dollar range like 'five to nine thousand', or a price for a single session.

decisions_for_mitch: Approved prices: confirm the only three prices are $3,600 (3 months, bi-weekly), $7,200 (3 months, weekly) and $14,000 (6 months, weekly), and whether any entry option (a paid first session, a deposit) is allowed. Today reps invent them: $1,000 first session on 15 calls, $2,400 starter on 9.

Setter price anchor: 'low to mid four figures' does not match $7,200 or $14,000, and setters drift to 'mid to high' or '5 to 9 thousand' on 16 of 18 calls. Pick one true anchor for every setter and DM script.
Success-rate claims: the '50% within six months, 78% within 12 months' and '80% find a partner' lines are said on 28 calls. Either document them with a real source or ban them.
Recording and retention: what happens to recordings of prospects who do not buy, so the closer's disclosure line can be accurate. Reps have promised deletion on 3 calls.
